# Continuous projective fiber charts: exact criteria and uniformization obstructions

This note studies a map that KEEPS the integer label z:

    T(z,X)=(z,X/L(z,X)).

It distinguishes it from the full projective map and from the previously
audited base-only rescaling K_z/ell_z in homogeneous coordinates. There
are exact legal subclasses and a useful homogeneous row identity, but
no automatic conversion of dm/L into uniform compatible convex fibers.
The counterexamples below concern this proposed construction; they are
not joint-minimum or OC counterexamples.

## 1. Archive boundary and the affine single-fiber calculation

The old `candidate 7bd76540986ac981` already proves that keeping
z while dividing only X by a BASE-only ell(z) can destroy convexity and
ambient halfspaces. It also gives the correct weighted measure and changed
lattice for the full map. The old
`candidate b0296f8a3b0d3d48`
has a different contact-weight/cone-volume calculation and a mass-level
Brunn--Minkowski obstruction. Neither licenses a continuous-denominator
fiber map. The new calculations here retain that denominator explicitly.

First suppose

    L(z,X)=ell(z)+c.X>0 on C,
    ell(z)=b+beta.z.                                   (1)

At a fixed base z,

    D_X(X/L)=L^(-1)Id-L^(-2)X c^T,
    det D_X(X/L)=ell(z)L^(-d-1).                       (2)

Thus positivity of L alone is NOT invertibility of this particular map.
For example, K=[1,2] and L(X)=X have X/L=1 throughout the positive fiber.
When ell(z) is nonzero the inverse on the fiber image is

    X=ell(z)Y/(1-c.Y),       1-c.Y=ell(z)/L(z,X).        (3)

The image of a convex fiber is then convex. In fact the image of a
segment is the same segment between the image endpoints, parametrized
by the positive weights proportional to their L values. This single-fiber
assertion permits either sign of nonzero ell(z); the positive chart in
Sections 2--4 uses ell(z)>0 to keep all inverse denominators positive.
Changing the continuous origin changes ell(z), but does not itself
establish any common affine center graph or anchored compatibility.

## 2. An exact anchored-inclusion criterion

Assume ell(z)>0 at every sampled base. For any anchored relation
q=sum_j lambda_j z_j and arbitrary X_j in K_zj, set

    L_j=L(z_j,X_j),
    D=sum_j lambda_j ell(z_j)/L_j>0.

The midpoint/convex combination of the IMAGE points has inverse in the
target fiber q equal to

    X_*=ell(q) [sum_j lambda_j X_j/L_j]/D.              (4)

Consequently the image family is compatible if and only if X_* belongs
to K_q for every such relation and input tuple. This is a changed-weight
condition, not the old inclusion sum lambda K_z subset K_q. To verify
(4), use sum lambda=1 to compute

    1-c.sum_j lambda_j(X_j/L_j)
                  =sum_j lambda_j ell(z_j)/L_j=D,

then apply (3). Since every image fiber is convex, it suffices to check
the extreme anchored representations and all input points for them.
General representations follow by linearity of the corresponding support
inequalities.

There is a scalar support version without inverse coordinates. For every
continuous normal v, the image support alpha_z(v) is the UNIQUE root of

    h_Kz(v-alpha c)=alpha ell(z).                      (5)

Indeed the difference of the two sides is
max_X[v.X-alpha L(z,X)], a continuous strictly decreasing function of
alpha with limits of opposite sign, since min_Kz L>0. The exact finite
base compatibility test is therefore

    alpha_q(v)>=sum_j lambda_j alpha_zj(v)             (6)

for every extreme anchored relation and every v. Equations (4)--(6)
are practical exact tests on polytopes: all fractional maxima in (5)
are attained at vertices. They do not turn original convexity into (6).

A nontrivial legal geometric subclass is

    K_z=ell(z)K,  ell>0 affine,
    L(z,X)=ell(z)+c.X,  1+c.x>0 on K.

Every image fiber is the SAME convex body {x/(1+c.x):x in K}; hence the
image is a compatible product family. This geometric fact alone does
not remove the density in Section 4 or preserve arbitrary oblique caps.

## 3. Exact failures of compatibility and of the cap family

For a genuinely continuous denominator, take the actual canonical family

    P={-1,0,1},   K_z=[z+2,5],   L(z,X)=1+X.           (7)

The fibers have lengths (4,3,2), and the old midpoint relation is exact
at the lower support. They are compatible intervals and L is positive
affine on the whole hull. Their label-preserving images are

    [1/2,5/6],    [2/3,5/6],    [3/4,5/6].            (8)

The midpoint of the lower endpoint image points at bases -1 and 1 is
5/8<2/3. Thus (8) is NOT compatible. This is not a base-only denominator
example. Every proper closed-minor quota holds in the ORIGINAL family:
its masses 4,3,2 are all below M/2=9/2 and the adjacent pair masses 7,5
are below M=9. Geometric normalization of L only rescales all image
fibers by a common positive factor and does not repair the failure.

For a general old halfspace a.z+u.X>=h, substitution of (3) gives the
EXACT closed image inequality

    a.z-h+[ell(z)u-(a.z-h)c].Y>=0.                    (9)

The new mixed quadratic coefficient is u beta^T-c a^T. Its vanishing is
a sufficient condition for this expression to be affine; it is not stated
as necessary for all possible factorizations on the positive chart.
Pure-base halfspaces, for example, remain the same base halfspaces after
canceling a positive factor. Arbitrary oblique halfspaces do not survive.

This failure is independent of (8). On the product [0,1]_z times [0,1]_X
with L=1+X the IMAGE BODY is the convex product [0,1] times [0,1/2].
But the old cap X>=z becomes

    Y>=z/(1+z).

It contains (0,0) and (1,1/2) but not their midpoint (1/2,1/4), since
1/4<1/3. Hence even this cap image is nonconvex. With the complete base
{0,1,2} instead, the old cap X>=(z+2)/8 gives image thresholds
1/5,3/11,1/3. All three upper traces are proper, and these thresholds
are not affine in z, so they cannot be one ambient halfspace at all
three unchanged labels.

## 4. The measure stays nonuniform, and finite convex lifts can be impossible

For affine L and ell(z)>0, (2) gives the exact pushforward of tilted
volume on each fiber:

    T_*(dX/L)=ell(z)^(d-1)(1-c.Y)^(-d) dY.             (10)

Thus the exponent d+1 from the projective Jacobian does not equal the
desired exponent 1. The chart does NOT uniformize the tilted volume.
On a compact positive chart its density is bounded, but the distortion
ratio may be as large as (L_max/L_min)^d within a fiber, with no universal
bound supplied by positivity alone. If c=0, the density is the fiberwise
constant ell(z)^(d-1); d=1 is the exceptional uniform case, still subject
to the already demonstrated geometry and halfspace failures.

There are two independent exact convex-lift obstructions.

First, even on ONE interval K=[0,1], L=1+X, (10) is the density
(1-Y)^(-1) on [0,1/2]. If it were the volume density of sections of a
convex body in ANY additional finite positive dimension r, the
Brunn--Minkowski theorem would make its r-th root concave. That root is
(1-Y)^(-1/r), strictly convex. Thus no finite-dimensional uniform convex
lift preserving this Y projection can realize the density. Transverse
shapes, translations, and a common positive multiplicative factor do not
alter this necessary section-volume condition.

Second, suppose only the total tilted masses at the original lattice
labels are to be preserved, allowing arbitrary new fiber shapes and
continuous dimension r. Start from THREE IDENTICAL volume-one fibers and
the base-affine L(z,X)=1+z/2 at P={-1,0,1}. Their tilted masses are

    (2,1,2/3).                                         (11)

For every finite r>0 the function z->(1+z/2)^(-1/r) is strictly convex,
so these masses violate the required midpoint Brunn--Minkowski inequality.
Hence no exact uniform compatible family at the same labels can realize
them, even after a common mass rescaling. This mass-level obstruction is
the exponent-one counterpart of the archived contact-weight obstruction;
it is not a new claim that the old construction was legal.

There is no universal two-sided distortion bound either. Replace the
three affine denominator values by (e,1,2-e), 0<e<1. If candidate compatible
r-dimensional volumes W_z approximate these tilted masses within a common
factor C>=1, up to one common positive scaling, midpoint BM forces

    C >= [(e^(-1/r)+(2-e)^(-1/r))/2]^(r/2)
      >= [e(2-e)]^(-1/4).                              (12)

The last bound tends to infinity even if r is freely chosen. Here
"within C" means nu_z/C<=W_z<=C nu_z after the common scaling. The
obstruction concerns arbitrary positive affine parameters; no stationarity
or deepest-source condition is claimed for these examples.

## 5. Finite-PL denominators can destroy convexity inside one fiber

Let K=[-1,1]^2 and

    L(X)=2-|X_1|=min(2-X_1,2+X_1)>0.                  (13)

The points (-1,1) and (1,1) map to themselves. Their midpoint (0,1)
would require an original point (0,2), because L=2 when X_1=0, and
therefore is not in the image. So the image of this SINGLE convex fiber
is nonconvex, although zero is an interior point and both affine pieces
have strictly positive constant term. This is not an injectivity failure:
along each ray, r/L(r omega) is strictly increasing on the available
interval. It is a failure of convexity itself.

On the interior of an active PL cell r, the local Jacobian is still

    det D_X(X/L)=ell_r(z)L^(-d-1).

One may use this cellwise formula with the area formula and the correct
preimage multiplicities. It is not a license to apply (10) globally when
the map folds, collapses, or has a nonconvex image. The example (13)
already blocks the proposed convex-fiber construction before any cap
or density argument.

## 6. What the full homogeneous lift actually preserves

There is nevertheless a clean exact lift. Put w=(z,X) and

    Psi(w)=(Z,Y,s)=(z,X,1)/L(w).                       (14)

For AFFINE positive L=b+beta.z+c.X, the full image Psi(C) is the convex
slice

    (Z,Y) in s C,  s>0,
    beta.Z+c.Y+b s=1.                                 (15)

Every old closed halfspace a.z+u.X>=h becomes exactly the homogeneous
halfspace a.Z+u.Y-h s>=0. The lift is injective because s>0 and its
inverse is (z,X)=(Z,Y)/s. No nonzero constant-term assumption is needed
for this embedding; that assumption is needed when coordinates are
dropped to a same-dimensional fractional map.

But an original integer fiber is now the d-plane piece

    Z=z s,    ell(z)s+c.Y=1.                           (16)

When c!=0 its base Z varies along the continuous fiber. These planes
are not a parallel family over the original lattice. Keeping their old
labels externally does not make them ordinary mixed-integer fibers.

For completeness the intrinsic d-dimensional Jacobian of (14), restricted
to the old fiber z, is

    J_Psi,z(X)=sqrt[ell(z)^2+(1+|z|^2)|c|^2] L^(-d-1). (17)

To prove (17), rotate c into the first continuous coordinate. After
factoring L^(-1) from each derivative column, the first exterior-product
component orthogonal to the other d-1 columns has continuous component
ell/L and extra-coordinate component -(z,1)|c|/L. This proves the norm
in (17), including ell=0. Accordingly dm/L again pushes to density
L^d/sqrt[ell(z)^2+(1+|z|^2)|c|^2] relative to intrinsic image volume;
it is generally nonuniform.

For PL concave L=min_r A_r, the graph Psi(C) lies on the boundary
min_r A_r^hom=1 of the convex set

    (Z,Y) in s C, s>0,   A_r^hom(Z,Y,s)>=1 for all r.

The graph itself need not be convex. A contact cell where L=A_r maps into
one genuine affine slice and is convex there. Enlarging the graph to the
whole displayed convex set changes dimension, measure, and cap law.

## 7. Exact original-volume martingale identity under the lift

Let an L-tight full-space volume row be a probability rho_i with source
Y_i, mean Y_i, and integral L d rho_i=L_i=L(Y_i). Define its original-volume
reweighting

    d bar_rho_i=(L/L_i)d rho_i.

Then bar_rho_i is a probability and the lifted barycenter identity is

    integral Psi(w) d bar_rho_i(w)
                      =(Y_i,1)/L_i=Psi(Y_i).           (18)

For the audited volume transport, sum_i sigma_i bar_rho_i=dm/M, so (18)
is an exact finite-source martingale whose target is the pushforward of
ORIGINAL mixed volume. It remains valid for PL L; each positive row is
confined to its affine contact cells, and thus to the corresponding
affine slice described in Section 6.

This is a legitimate projective row identity. Its price is explicit:
the target is not uniform intrinsic volume by (17), the old fibers sit
in nonparallel planes (16), and the source-count/parity structure has not
become a new lattice. None of these facts is removed by the equality of
the lifted barycenters. Thus (18) can be used as an exact bookkeeping
identity, but cannot be substituted for a mixed uniform-body theorem.

The companion `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_continuous_projective_fiber_obstructions_slab_recovery.py`
passes 492 exact chart, determinant/Gram-Jacobian, anchored inverse,
strict-quota, halfspace-trace, and homogeneous-row checks. The arbitrary
dimension lift obstruction follows from the displayed strict-convexity
and Brunn--Minkowski proof, not from finite-dimensional sampling.
